title: SQL Day 10 — Advanced Subqueries, Correlated Logic & CTE Foundations
description: Move from nested SQL to readable multi-step analysis using derived tables, correlated subqueries, nested aggregation, and CTEs.

topics.title: Derived Tables — Subquery as a Dataset
topics.business_skill: Create a temporary result set that can be queried like a table.

teaching.teacher: ## Derived table\nA subquery in FROM produces a temporary result set that the outer query can filter, join, or aggregate.
teaching.explain: Use derived tables when an intermediate dataset is itself part of the business logic.
teaching.detailedlearning: Give the derived table an alias and keep its output columns focused.
teaching.expose: A derived table is useful when you need to aggregate first and analyze second.
teaching.example: SELECT region,total_sales FROM (SELECT region,SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY region) x;
teaching.business_question: The director wants to rank regions after first calculating regional sales.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT region,total_sales FROM (SELECT region,SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY region) x ORDER BY total_sales DESC;

questions.scenario: Management wants a regional sales table sorted highest first.
questions.request: First calculate regional sales, then return the result in descending sales order.

questions.scenario: Finance wants only categories whose aggregated profit is positive.
questions.request: Create a category profit dataset and filter it to positive-profit categories.

questions.scenario: The report needs customer totals and a ranking-ready intermediate dataset.
questions.request: Create a customer-level sales dataset containing customer ID and total sales.

topics.title: Correlated Subqueries
topics.business_skill: Compare each row against a related benchmark calculated for that row's group.

teaching.teacher: ## Correlated subquery\nThe inner query references a column from the outer query, so it is evaluated in the context of the current outer row.
teaching.explain: This supports rules such as 'orders above their customer's average order value'.
teaching.detailedlearning: Identify the outer row and the related population before writing the correlation.
teaching.expose: Correlation is powerful but can be expensive on large datasets; consider CTE/window alternatives later.
teaching.example: SELECT o.order_id,o.customer_id,o.sales FROM orders o WHERE o.sales > (SELECT AVG(o2.sales) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.customer_id=o.customer_id);
teaching.business_question: The manager wants orders above their customer's average order value.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT o.order_id,o.customer_id,o.sales FROM orders o WHERE o.sales > (SELECT AVG(o2.sales) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.customer_id=o.customer_id);

questions.scenario: The team wants orders above each customer's own average order value.
questions.request: Return order ID, customer ID, and sales for orders above that customer's average.

questions.scenario: The manager wants orders above the average order value within their region.
questions.request: Return order ID, region, and sales above the corresponding regional average.

questions.scenario: Product management wants products whose order sales exceed the average sale for that product.
questions.request: Return order ID, product ID, and sales above the product-level average.

topics.title: Correlated EXISTS
topics.business_skill: Test related business conditions for each outer record.

teaching.teacher: ## Correlated EXISTS\nEXISTS can reference outer columns to test whether a related record satisfying a condition exists.
teaching.explain: This is useful for questions such as customers who have at least one profitable order.
teaching.detailedlearning: The inner query should contain the relationship plus the specific business condition.
teaching.expose: EXISTS stops conceptually at the first match, making it ideal for existence tests.
teaching.example: SELECT c.customer_id,c.customer_name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.customer_id AND o.profit>0);
teaching.business_question: Customer leadership wants customers with at least one profitable order.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT c.customer_id,c.customer_name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.customer_id AND o.profit>0);

questions.scenario: The director wants customers with at least one profitable transaction.
questions.request: Return customers for whom a profitable order exists.

questions.scenario: Leadership wants customers with at least one Technology order.
questions.request: Return customers with a Technology purchase.

questions.scenario: The team wants customers with no recent? Use no date assumption. Instead customers with no loss-making order.
questions.request: Return customers for whom no loss-making order exists.

topics.title: Nested Aggregation
topics.business_skill: Aggregate an aggregated dataset to answer second-level KPI questions.

teaching.teacher: ## Nested aggregation\nFirst calculate a metric at one grain, then aggregate that result at a higher level.
teaching.explain: Examples include average customer sales, maximum regional sales, or average category profit.
teaching.detailedlearning: The inner query establishes the correct lower-level grain.
teaching.expose: Do not calculate an average of raw rows when the business asks for an average of customer totals.
teaching.example: SELECT AVG(customer_sales) FROM (SELECT customer_id,SUM(sales) AS customer_sales FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) x;
teaching.business_question: The director wants the average total sales per customer.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT AVG(customer_sales) AS avg_customer_sales FROM (SELECT customer_id,SUM(sales) AS customer_sales FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) x;

questions.scenario: Management wants average total sales per customer.
questions.request: Return the average of customer-level sales totals.

questions.scenario: Leadership wants the average regional sales total.
questions.request: Return the average of region-level sales totals.

questions.scenario: The executive report needs the maximum customer sales total.
questions.request: Return the highest total sales generated by any customer.

topics.title: CTE Foundations
topics.business_skill: Replace complex nested queries with named, readable analysis layers.

teaching.teacher: ## CTE\nWITH creates a named temporary result set that can be referenced by the following query.
teaching.explain: CTEs improve readability by giving each business calculation a name.
teaching.detailedlearning: Use one CTE per logical transformation and then write the final SELECT against those layers.
teaching.expose: A CTE is a readability and modularity tool; it does not automatically materialize data.
teaching.example: WITH regional_sales AS (SELECT region,SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY region) SELECT * FROM regional_sales ORDER BY total_sales DESC;
teaching.business_question: The director wants a clean query that first calculates regional sales and then sorts them.
teaching.expected_sql: WITH regional_sales AS (SELECT region,SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY region) SELECT region,total_sales FROM regional_sales ORDER BY total_sales DESC;

questions.scenario: The report needs a named regional sales layer.
questions.request: Create a CTE for regional sales and return the results.

questions.scenario: Finance wants categories above the average category profit using readable SQL.
questions.request: Build a category-profit CTE, calculate its average, and return categories above that benchmark.

questions.scenario: The executive KPI needs customer totals joined to customer attributes.
questions.request: Create a customer-sales CTE and join it to customers to return customer name, segment, and total sales.
